title: The Lunchbox Detective
summary_zh: 两个一样的午餐盒引出一场小侦探游戏：怎样用线索找到主人？
story:
At Maple School, Maya puts a blue lunchbox on the table. Leo puts another blue lunchbox beside it. They look exactly the same.

Is this yours? Maya asks.

I think so, Leo says. He opens it. Inside are rice, carrots, and an egg. That is strange. My dad made me a sandwich.

Then this one is mine, says Maya. But wait. My lunch has noodles today.

Now they have two lunchboxes and no lunch they recognize. Pip, their small classroom robot, rolls over. I have a solution. Eat both lunches.

That is not a solution, says Maya. That is your lunch plan.

Ms. Park asks them to look for clues without eating anything. One box has a tiny star on the bottom. The other has a name under the handle.

This says Sam, Leo reads. So it is his.

A girl named June arrives. The star is mine, she says. My brother drew it.

Maya looks under the table. There is her lunchbox, still inside her backpack. Leo checks his bag, too. His sandwich is there.

We were looking at their lunches, says Maya, but we did not check our own bags.

Pip thinks for a moment. My first clue is that I am still hungry.

You do not eat sandwiches, Leo tells him.

Correct, says Pip. But I can appreciate a good mystery.
fact: A clue is something that helps you answer a question. Evidence supports an idea. A blue box is a weak clue when many people have blue boxes. A name label is stronger evidence. Good detectives check their ideas before deciding they are right.
recap: Maya and Leo saw two blue lunchboxes and guessed they were theirs. Labels showed that the boxes belonged to Sam and June. Their own lunches were still in their bags. Looking carefully solved the mystery.
question: What finally helped the children find the owners: the color or the labels?
answer: The labels helped them. Both boxes were blue, so color alone was not enough.
wonder: If you had to describe your backpack without using its color, what clues would you give?

title: Pip and the Upside-Down Library
summary_zh: Pip按书的颜色整理书架，却让大家找不到书。好用的分类需要什么规则？
story:
The school library needs help. Books are on tables, chairs, and even a windowsill. Pip is excited. I can sort them, he says.

When Maya returns, every shelf looks beautiful. Red books are together. Blue books are together. One green book sits beside a green plant.

Where is the book about sharks? she asks.

What color is it? Pip replies.

I do not remember.

Then we have a small problem.

Leo wants a story by his favorite author. Pip asks whether the cover is dark blue or light blue. Leo does not know that either.

Ms. Park brings three books to the table. One is about whales. One is about the Moon. One is a story about a whale visiting the Moon.

They all have blue covers, Maya says, but their subjects are different.

The librarian explains their system. Stories are in one section. Books that explain real things are in another. Signs and labels help readers find smaller groups.

Let me help you, Leo says to Pip. They check the labels together and move the books. The shark book joins the animal books. The Moon book joins the space books.

Where do I put the plant? Pip asks.

By the window, says the librarian.

Pip adds a little sign: Not a book. Please do not return it through the book slot.
fact: Sorting means putting things into groups using a rule. You can sort the same objects in different ways: by size, color, or purpose. A useful system depends on what you need to find. Libraries use organized systems and labels so that other people can follow the rules, too.
recap: Pip sorted books by color. The shelves looked nice, but readers could not easily find a subject or an author. The children followed the library's labels instead. A good sorting rule helps people do a job.
phrases: Let me help you sort them.
question: Why was sorting only by color a problem?
answer: Readers often knew a subject or an author, but they did not remember the color of the cover.
wonder: How would you organize a box of toys so that a friend could find one quickly?

title: The Paper Bridge Challenge
summary_zh: 同样一张纸，改变形状能否让桥更结实？
story:
The science club has a challenge. Build a bridge between two books using one sheet of paper. Then see how many small blocks it can hold.

Leo lays his paper flat. This is a very fast bridge, he says.

The first block stays on it. The second block makes the middle bend. The third block falls through, taking the bridge with it.

Fast to build, Maya says, and fast to fall.

Pip offers to hold the paper up. Ms. Park smiles. The bridge has to work without a robot underneath it.

Maya folds her paper back and forth, like a small fan. She puts it across the same gap. It holds more blocks before it bends.

Did you use thicker paper? Leo asks.

No. We used the same kind. I changed the shape.

Leo wants to make the gap smaller, add tape, and use two sheets at once.

Let us change one thing first, says Maya. Then we can understand what helped.

They fold a new sheet and test it over the original gap. This time, they write down the result. They also put the blocks in the same place each time.

Pip names the bridge The Great Paper Highway.

Can a bus cross it? he asks.

A toy bus, perhaps, says Leo.

Pip makes a sign: Small vehicles only. Large robots must go around.
fact: An object's shape can affect how it bends under a load. Folding paper can make it harder to bend in some directions. Engineers compare designs, test them, and improve them. When you change one feature at a time, it is easier to understand why a result changed.
recap: A flat paper bridge bent quickly. Maya folded the paper and tested it across the same gap. The new shape held more blocks in their test. The club learned to compare designs carefully and keep a record.
phrases: We used the same kind of paper.
question: What did Maya change in the first improved bridge?
answer: She changed the shape by folding the paper. She did not use a thicker sheet.
wonder: Where can you see folds, curves, or triangles in things that need to be strong?

title: The Mystery Humming Box
summary_zh: 音乐教室里的盒子为什么会嗡嗡响？
story:
A strange humming sound comes from the music room. Maya stops outside the door. Is someone singing inside a box?

Leo listens. It sounds like a very small monster with a cold.

They knock and enter. Their music teacher is holding an empty tissue box with rubber bands stretched around it.

Meet my new instrument, she says.

Pip looks into the box. No monster detected.

The teacher gently plucks a rubber band. It moves back and forth so quickly that its middle looks blurry. The box makes a soft musical sound.

That movement is called vibration, she explains. The moving band makes the air around it vibrate, too.

Maya touches the band gently. The movement stops, and the sound stops.

Leo tries a tighter band. It makes a higher sound. He tries again, listening carefully.

Can we play a song? Maya asks.

You can try, says the teacher, but first listen to the notes you have.

Their first song is not beautiful. Pip calls it A Robot Falling Down the Stairs. Their second song is better.

Maya hums along and puts a hand lightly on her throat. She feels a tiny movement.

My voice makes vibrations, too!

Pip records the concert. He saves it under Music, then thinks for a moment and adds a second label: Very Interesting Noise.
fact: Sound begins with vibration. Moving objects can make nearby air vibrate, and those changes travel to our ears. Vocal folds in your throat vibrate when you speak. A tighter string usually makes a higher note when its other important features stay the same.
recap: The mystery sound came from a rubber-band instrument. When the band vibrated, the children heard a note. When Maya stopped the movement, the note stopped. They discovered that their own voices involve vibration, too.
question: What happened when Maya gently stopped the rubber band from moving?
answer: The sound stopped because the rubber band was no longer vibrating.
wonder: Which objects around you vibrate when they make a sound?

title: Pancakes with Tiny Rooms
summary_zh: 松软煎饼里的小孔从哪里来？
story:
Today the cooking club is making pancakes. An adult handles the hot pan. Maya reads the recipe, and Leo measures the ingredients.

Pip wants to help. I have added an important ingredient, he announces.

What ingredient? asks Maya.

Encouragement. You are doing very well.

They mix flour, milk, an egg, and a little baking powder. Leo sees bubbles appearing in the batter.

Is it breathing? he asks.

No, says Ms. Park. The baking powder helps make gas. That gas forms bubbles.

When the first pancake is ready, she cuts it open. Inside are many tiny holes.

It has rooms! says Maya.

Can I move in? Pip asks.

Only if you become much smaller, Leo says.

They compare the fluffy pancake with a thin piece that has fewer little spaces. The textures feel different.

Maya writes a note for the club: Tiny bubbles can make a big difference.

Leo wants to add ten times as much baking powder. Then we could make the tallest pancake in the world.

Ms. Park shakes her head. More is not always better. Recipes use amounts that work together.

Pip makes a menu. Today's special: a pancake with many rooms, no windows, and a very short life.

Why a short life? Maya asks.

Because Leo is about to eat it.
fact: Baking powder can release carbon dioxide gas when it becomes wet, and many kinds release more when heated. Bubbles help batter rise. As the pancake cooks, its structure firms up around tiny spaces. Those spaces help make the pancake feel light and soft.
recap: The cooking club found tiny holes inside a pancake. Gas bubbles helped create those spaces. They followed a recipe instead of simply adding more baking powder. Pip supplied encouragement, but no real ingredients.
question: What helped make the tiny spaces inside the pancake?
answer: Gas bubbles in the batter helped make the spaces as the pancake cooked.
wonder: What other foods have little holes or bubbles inside them?

title: The Map with a Missing Key
summary_zh: 地图上的星星真的是宝藏吗？先读懂符号的意思。
story:
Maya finds a map for the school treasure hunt. A star sits beside a square. A blue line crosses the page. Three green circles stand near the bottom.

The star must be treasure, says Leo.

Pip disagrees. It could be a spaceship parking area.

They walk to the place marked with a star. It is the school office. There is no treasure, and the secretary has not seen any spaceships.

Do you have the map key? she asks.

We do not need a key, says Leo. Nothing is locked.

A map key explains the symbols, she tells him. It is also called a legend.

Maya unfolds the bottom of the paper. There it is. The star means information desk. The square means building. The blue line is a stream, and the green circles are large trees.

Now the first clue makes sense. Start at the information desk. Turn right at the stream. Look beside the three trees.

They follow the instructions and find a small box. Inside is the next clue.

Pip looks proud. My navigation system is excellent.

You thought the office was a spaceship parking area, Leo reminds him.

That possibility has now been removed, says Pip.

Maya puts the map away carefully, with the key still visible. This time, they know what their information means.
fact: Maps use symbols to show places without drawing every detail. A map key explains those symbols. A direction arrow can help you orient the map. Symbols are useful only when readers know what they mean; a star does not always mean the same thing on every map.
recap: The children guessed what the map's symbols meant and went to the wrong place. After reading the key, they understood the star, stream, and trees. Clear meanings turned a confusing picture into useful directions.
phrases: Excuse me. Where is the office?
It is next to the trees.
question: What did the star mean on this particular map?
answer: It meant the information desk. The map key explained its meaning.
wonder: What symbol would you invent for a quiet reading spot? How would you explain it?

title: A Day for a Tiny Planet
summary_zh: 用地球仪和灯，弄明白为什么一边白天、一边黑夜。
story:
Leo draws a picture of the Sun going to bed. It wears pajamas and carries a toothbrush.

Is that why it gets dark? Pip asks.

In my picture, yes, says Leo. In real life, probably not.

Ms. Park puts a globe beside a lamp. The lamp represents the Sun. She places a small sticker on the globe for their school.

At first, the sticker faces the lamp. This side is receiving sunlight, Maya says.

Then Ms. Park turns the globe. The sticker moves into the dark side.

Did the lamp turn off? she asks.

No. Our part of the globe turned away, says Leo.

They slowly rotate the globe again. Their school moves back into the light.

Good morning, tiny school, says Pip. I hope your tiny students remembered their homework.

Maya adds another sticker on a distant part of the globe. When our sticker is in the light, that one can be in the dark.

So people do not all eat breakfast at the same moment, Leo says.

Pip is worried. How do I know when to announce lunch?

Use the clock where you are, says Maya.

Leo changes his drawing. Now the Sun stays in place while a little Earth turns beside it. He keeps the pajamas in one corner.

Those are for me, he explains. Learning about night has made me sleepy.
fact: Earth rotates. A full turn relative to the Sun takes about twenty-four hours, giving us the familiar day-and-night cycle. The side facing the Sun has daylight; the side facing away has night. Earth's yearly trip around the Sun is a different movement.
recap: A lamp and a globe helped the club model day and night. Their school sticker moved into light and then darkness as the globe turned. The Sun did not need to switch off or go to bed.
phrases: What time is it where you are?
Our part of Earth is turning away.
question: What movement mainly causes day and night on Earth?
answer: Earth's rotation causes different parts of its surface to face toward or away from the Sun.
wonder: If you could call a friend on the other side of Earth, what might that friend be doing?

title: The Dinosaur at the Window
summary_zh: 博物馆里的恐龙和窗外的小鸟，竟然存在联系。

words.relative: 亲属；有亲缘关系的生物

story:
At the museum, Maya stands under an enormous dinosaur skeleton. Leo looks at its teeth.

I am glad it does not want my sandwich, he says.

Pip reads a sign. Some dinosaurs had feathers.

Like a chicken? asks Maya.

The guide smiles. Birds belong to a branch of the dinosaur family tree. They are living dinosaurs.

Leo looks toward the window. A small bird is sitting outside.

That little bird?

Yes, says the guide. Not every dinosaur was huge. Scientists compare fossils and living animals to understand their relationships.

Pip imagines the little bird carrying the giant skeleton away. His screen displays a warning: Size mismatch.

Being related does not mean being the same size, Maya tells him.

The guide shows them a fossil with marks left by feathers. They cannot hear the animal or see it move, but the fossil preserves clues from long ago.

Did this dinosaur sound like a duck? Leo asks.

That is an interesting question, says the guide. We cannot know every ancient sound just by looking at bones.

Outside, the little bird chirps. Leo holds his sandwich close.

I respect your family history, he tells the bird, but this lunch is mine.

Pip writes in his museum notebook: Today we met a giant dinosaur indoors and a very small living one outdoors.
fact: Modern birds evolved within a group of dinosaurs. Fossils can preserve bones, footprints, and sometimes impressions of feathers. They provide evidence about ancient life, but they do not answer every question. Scientists separate what evidence supports from what remains uncertain.
recap: The museum visit connected a huge skeleton with a small bird outside. Birds are part of the dinosaur family tree. Fossils helped scientists discover that relationship, while some questions, such as many ancient sounds, remain difficult to answer.
phrases: What was it like long ago?
They are related, but they are different.
question: Are all dinosaurs completely gone from Earth?
answer: No. Modern birds are living members of the dinosaur family tree, although the other dinosaur groups died out.
wonder: What would you ask a scientist who studies fossils?
